checks.label: AppOps: private-data access
checks.description: Apps with access to external storage or fine location - evidence collector, review for suspicious entries.
checks.remediation: Revoke permissions for suspicious apps: appops set <package> <op> ignore

checks.label: Security Tools Detected
checks.description: Pentest frameworks or hacking tools found
checks.remediation: Uninstall detected pentest tools: pm uninstall <package>

checks.label: Apps Installed Last 7 Days
checks.command: current=$(date +%s); for pkg in $(pm list packages -3 2>/dev/null | cut -d: -f2 | head -15); do ft=$(dumpsys package $pkg 2>/dev/null | grep firstInstallTime | grep -oE '[0-9]+' | head -1); [ -n "$ft" ] && d=$(( (current - ft/1000) / 86400 )) && [ $d -lt 7 ] && echo "$pkg (${d}d)"; done
checks.description: Third-party apps installed in last 7 days - review for legitimacy
checks.remediation: Review each recently installed app and uninstall any unauthorized ones: pm uninstall <package>

checks.label: Apps Not From Play Store
checks.command: pm list packages -3 -i 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'installer=com.android.vending' | grep -v 'installer=com.google' | head -10
checks.description: Apps installed from non-Play Store sources - higher malware risk
checks.remediation: Uninstall sideloaded apps: pm uninstall <package>. Disable unknown sources to prevent future installs.

checks.label: APK Signature Path Check
checks.description: Checks for valid APK path info
checks.remediation: If no valid APK path is returned, verify package integrity with: pm verify <package>

checks.label: Suspicious APK Names
checks.description: Packages with suspicious names
checks.remediation: Uninstall suspicious packages immediately: pm uninstall <package>

checks.label: Debuggable Apps (Strict)
checks.command: for pkg in $(pm list packages -3 2>/dev/null | cut -d: -f2 | head -20); do dumpsys package $pkg 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'DEBUGGABLE' && echo $pkg; done
checks.description: Third-party apps with debuggable flag enabled
checks.remediation: Uninstall debuggable apps: pm uninstall <package>. Replace with release (non-debug) builds.

checks.label: APK Signature Verification
checks.description: APK signatures must be verified
checks.remediation: Enable package verification: settings put global package_verifier_enable 1

checks.label: Dynamic Code Loading
checks.description: Apps should not use dynamic code loading (security risk)
checks.remediation: Uninstall apps using dynamic code loading: pm uninstall <package>

checks.label: Navigation Apps
checks.description: Navigation applications tracking location
checks.remediation: Revoke location access for unneeded nav apps: pm revoke <package> android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION

checks.label: Device Classification Properties
checks.command: getprop ro.product.device 2>/dev/null; getprop ro.product.model 2>/dev/null; getprop ro.product.manufacturer 2>/dev/null
checks.description: Device identification - document for regulatory purposes
checks.remediation: Record device model and manufacturer for asset inventory and compliance documentation.

checks.label: Root Access (su)
checks.command: su -c 'id' 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'uid=0' && echo 'ROOT_ACTIVE' || which su 2>/dev/null | grep -v '/system/bin/su'
checks.description: Check for actual root shell access (excludes Samsung system su)
checks.remediation: Remove root access by uninstalling su binary or root manager (e.g., pm uninstall com.topjohnwu.magisk).

checks.label: Running Services Count
checks.description: Running services on device
checks.remediation: Review running services and stop unnecessary ones: am stopservice <component>

checks.label: Xposed Framework
checks.command: P=$(pm list packages 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'xposed'); if [ -n "$P" ]; then printf '%s\n' "$P"; elif pm list packages >/dev/null 2>&1; then :; else strings -a /data/system/packages.xml 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'xposed' | sort -u; fi
checks.description: Xposed framework enables deep system tweaks
checks.remediation: Uninstall Xposed framework and modules: pm uninstall de.robv.android.xposed.installer

checks.label: Unapproved APKs in /data/local/tmp
checks.description: Unauthorized sideloading or testing APKs
checks.remediation: Delete unapproved APKs: rm /data/local/tmp/*.apk

checks.label: Running Services List
checks.description: All running processes - review for unnecessary services
checks.remediation: Kill unnecessary processes: kill <pid>. Disable unwanted services from auto-starting.

checks.label: Web Server Process
checks.description: Web server running - potential attack surface
checks.remediation: Stop and disable the web server if not required: kill <pid>. Remove the binary if unnecessary.

checks.label: Telnet Daemon
checks.description: Telnet daemon running - INSECURE!
checks.remediation: Kill telnet daemon immediately: kill <pid>. Replace with SSH for remote access.

checks.label: FTP Daemon
checks.description: FTP daemon running - credentials in plaintext!
checks.remediation: Kill FTP daemon immediately: kill <pid>. Replace with SFTP or SCP for secure file transfer.

checks.label: SSH Daemon
checks.description: SSH daemon running
checks.remediation: Ensure SSH uses key-based auth and disable password login. Restrict access with AllowUsers directive.

checks.label: MQTT Client/Broker
checks.description: MQTT service running
checks.remediation: Ensure MQTT uses TLS and authentication. Disable anonymous access in broker config.

checks.label: Node.js/Python Services
checks.description: Script-based services running
checks.remediation: Audit script-based services for known vulnerabilities. Update runtimes to latest patched versions.

checks.label: Database Services
checks.description: Database services running
checks.remediation: Ensure databases require authentication and are not exposed on public interfaces. Bind to localhost only.

checks.label: Docker/Container Runtime
checks.description: Container runtime detected
checks.remediation: Audit running containers for outdated images. Restrict Docker socket access to authorized users only.

checks.label: Init System Type
checks.description: Init system (systemd/init/busybox)
checks.remediation: Document the init system type. Review startup services for unnecessary or insecure daemons.

checks.label: Custom IoT Daemons
checks.description: Non-Android services/daemons running
checks.remediation: Audit each custom daemon for necessity and security. Disable unneeded ones via init scripts.

checks.label: Camera Permission Apps
checks.description: Apps with camera permission
checks.remediation: Revoke camera from untrusted apps: pm revoke <package> android.permission.CAMERA

checks.label: Microphone Permission Apps
checks.description: Apps with microphone permission
checks.remediation: Revoke microphone from untrusted apps: pm revoke <package> android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO

checks.label: Location Permission Apps
checks.description: Apps with fine location permission
checks.remediation: Revoke location from untrusted apps: pm revoke <package> android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION

checks.label: SMS Permission Apps
checks.description: Apps with SMS sending permission
checks.remediation: Revoke SMS permission from non-essential apps: pm revoke <package> android.permission.SEND_SMS

checks.label: Contacts Permission Apps
checks.description: Apps with contacts read permission
checks.remediation: Revoke contacts access from untrusted apps: pm revoke <package> android.permission.READ_CONTACTS

checks.label: Unknown Sources Disabled
checks.command: SDK=$(getprop ro.build.version.sdk 2>/dev/null); V=$(settings get secure install_non_market_apps 2>/dev/null); if [ -n "$SDK" ] && [ "$SDK" -ge 26 ] 2>/dev/null; then echo "PER_APP_MODEL sdk=$SDK legacy_flag=${V:-null}"; else echo "${V:-null}"; fi
checks.description: Reports the legacy global unknown-sources setting. From Android 8 (API 26) this setting no longer controls anything: sideloading is governed per app by the REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES permission, which the companion check in this category audits. A stale value of 1 is a leftover from an earlier Android version and is not a finding, so on API 26 and above this reports PER_APP_MODEL and passes. Verified on a reference Android device running API 31 where the legacy flag was 1 while the per-app model was in force.
checks.remediation: Disable unknown sources: settings put secure install_non_market_apps 0

checks.label: Play Protect Enabled
checks.description: Google Play Protect consent status
checks.remediation: Enable Play Protect: settings put global package_verifier_user_consent 1

checks.label: Install via ADB Blocked
checks.description: Block app installation via ADB
checks.remediation: Block ADB installs: settings put global install_allow_adb 0

checks.label: Permission Controller Version
checks.command: dumpsys package com.google.android.permissioncontroller 2>/dev/null | grep versionName | head -1
checks.description: Permission controller app version
checks.remediation: Update the permission controller via Play Store to ensure latest security patches are applied.

checks.label: Auto Revoke Unused Permissions
checks.description: Auto-revoke permissions for unused apps
checks.remediation: Enable auto-revoke: settings put global auto_revoke_permissions_mode 2

checks.label: Background Location Apps
checks.description: Apps with background location access
checks.remediation: Revoke background location: appops set <package> android:coarse_location deny

checks.label: Camera Apps Running
checks.description: Apps currently using camera
checks.remediation: Force-stop apps using the camera unexpectedly: am force-stop <package>

checks.label: Overlay Permission (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW)
checks.command: DUMP=$(dumpsys package 2>/dev/null); for pkg in $(pm list packages -3 2>/dev/null | cut -d: -f2 | head -30); do echo "$DUMP" | grep -A200 "Package.*$pkg" | head -200 | grep -q 'SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW.*granted=true' && echo "OVERLAY: $pkg"; done
checks.description: Third-party apps with draw-over-other-apps permission - enables phishing overlay attacks on POS/banking screens
checks.remediation: Revoke overlay permission: appops set <package> SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW deny

checks.label: Current Foreground Window
checks.description: Currently focused window and app - useful for detecting active overlay attacks in real-time
checks.remediation: If an unexpected app is in the foreground, force-stop it: am force-stop <package>

checks.label: Backup-Enabled Apps (allowBackup)
checks.command: for pkg in $(pm list packages -3 2>/dev/null | cut -d: -f2 | head -20); do dumpsys package $pkg 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'allowBackup=true' && echo "BACKUP_ON: $pkg"; done
checks.description: Third-party apps with allowBackup=true - ADB backup can extract app data including credentials and tokens
checks.remediation: Disable ADB backup globally: settings put secure backup_enabled 0. Contact app developers to set allowBackup=false.

checks.label: Frida Detected
checks.description: Frida binary indicates runtime manipulation
checks.remediation: Uninstall Frida: pm uninstall <frida-package>. Remove frida-server binary from /data/local/tmp.

checks.label: Magisk Detected
checks.description: Magisk can hide root access
checks.remediation: Uninstall Magisk: pm uninstall com.topjohnwu.magisk. Reflash stock boot image to fully remove root.

checks.label: Third-party Shared UID Packages
checks.description: Non-system apps sharing UIDs may indicate privilege escalation risk. Apps sharing a UID run in the same process sandbox and can access each other's data.
checks.remediation: Uninstall apps sharing UIDs unless they are from the same trusted vendor: pm uninstall <package>

checks.label: System Apps Signed with v1-only Signature Scheme
checks.command: for pkg in $(pm list packages -s 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^package://' | head -50); do info=$(dumpsys package "$pkg" 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'signatures=|signingInfo' | head -1); echo "$pkg: $info"; done | grep -i 'v1' | head -10
checks.description: System apps signed only with the JAR (v1) signature scheme are vulnerable to Janus-style (CVE-2017-13156) tampering. Modern apps should use signature scheme v2 or v3 (or v4 with incremental). Empty output means no v1-only system apps were found in the sampled set.
checks.remediation: Ensure all system apps are signed with APK signature scheme v2 or v3. Rebuild or re-sign affected apps using apksigner with --v2-signing-enabled and --v3-signing-enabled.

checks.label: Apps Requesting QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES
checks.command: pm list packages -U 2>/dev/null | head -1 >/dev/null; for pkg in $(pm list packages 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^package://' | head -200); do dumpsys package "$pkg" 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES' && echo "$pkg"; done | head -20
checks.description: QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES (Android 11+) lets an app enumerate every installed package on the device, bypassing the new package-visibility restrictions. Legitimate uses are narrow (launchers, antivirus). Many sideloaded or adware apps abuse it.
checks.remediation: Review each listed app. Uninstall or revoke the permission for any app whose legitimate function does not require enumerating all installed packages.

checks.label: Apps Requesting REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES
checks.command: for pkg in $(pm list packages 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^package://' | head -200); do dumpsys package "$pkg" 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES' && echo "$pkg"; done | head -20
checks.description: REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES lets an app prompt the user to sideload APKs. Necessary for app stores, browsers, and file managers; abused by malware to drop payloads. On a locked-down kiosk or POS device the list should ideally be empty or limited to the OEM updater.
checks.remediation: Review each listed app. On kiosk/POS devices, restrict this permission to the OEM update agent only; revoke it for browsers, file managers, and unknown apps.

checks.label: Sandboxed SDK Runtime (Privacy Sandbox)
checks.command: SDK=$(getprop ro.build.version.sdk 2>/dev/null); if [ -z "$SDK" ] || [ "$SDK" -lt 33 ] 2>/dev/null; then echo "PRE_A13_SDK_$SDK"; else P=$(pm list packages 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'sdksandbox|adservices' | sed 's/^package://' | tr '\n' ' '); echo "sdk=$SDK runtime=${P:-not_present}"; fi
checks.description: The SDK Runtime, part of Privacy Sandbox on Android, moves third-party advertising and analytics SDKs out of the host app process into a separate sandboxed process with its own restricted permissions and no access to the host app's storage or non-sandboxed permissions. This reports whether the SDK Runtime and AdServices packages are installed. It matters for audit scope: when the runtime is active, an SDK's data access is no longer implied by the host app's manifest permissions, so an app permission review alone no longer describes what a bundled SDK can reach. Informational, since the runtime's presence depends on the Android version and whether the build ships GMS.
checks.remediation: Nothing to fix on-device. When reviewing app permissions on a device with the SDK Runtime present, audit sandboxed SDK permissions separately from host app permissions rather than assuming the host manifest covers both.

checks.label: Hidden API Enforcement Not Disabled
checks.command: V=$(settings get global hidden_api_policy 2>/dev/null); P=$(settings get global hidden_api_policy_p_apps 2>/dev/null); echo "policy=${V:-null} p_apps=${P:-null}"
checks.description: Android restricts app access to non-SDK framework interfaces. The hidden_api_policy setting overrides that: 0 or unset keeps the default enforcement, 1 warns only, 2 and 3 permit access to dark-grey and blacklisted APIs. It is a developer and instrumentation aid, and a production device with it set to a non-zero value has had the restriction lifted for every app, widening the framework surface any installed app can reach. A non-null, non-zero value is also a strong indicator the device has been prepared for reverse engineering.
checks.remediation: Reset with 'settings delete global hidden_api_policy' and confirm no MDM or init script re-applies it. Investigate why it was set on a production device.
checks.why: Disabling hidden API enforcement gives every installed app access to non-SDK framework interfaces that the platform deliberately restricts.
checks.risk_if_fail: Any app can reach internal framework APIs, widening the attack surface and defeating a platform containment control.

checks.label: Packages Running As System UID
checks.command: pm list packages -U 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'uid:1000$|uid:1000 ' | sed 's/package://' | head -15; [ $? -ne 0 ] && dumpsys package 2>/dev/null | grep -B2 'userId=1000' | grep -oE 'Package \[[^]]+\]' | head -15
checks.description: Lists packages sharing the system UID (1000). A package running as system holds the privileges of the platform itself and must be signed with the platform key, so the set should be small and consist only of core OEM system components. Each additional package running as system is a full-privilege attack surface: a vulnerability in any of them is a system compromise, with no sandbox boundary to cross. Reported for review because the legitimate set is entirely OEM-specific.
checks.remediation: Review each package against the OEM's documented system components. Any third-party or unexpected package running as system UID should be treated as a critical finding and investigated for how it obtained platform signing.

checks.label: Privileged App Permission Allowlist
checks.command: F=$(ls /system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions*.xml /vendor/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions*.xml /product/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions*.xml 2>/dev/null | wc -l); N=$(cat /system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions*.xml /vendor/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions*.xml 2>/dev/null | grep -c '<permission'); echo "allowlist_files=${F:-0} granted_permissions=${N:-0}"
checks.description: Counts the privapp-permissions allowlist files and the privileged permissions they grant. Since Android 9 a privileged app in /system/priv-app only receives a signature-or-privileged permission if it is explicitly allowlisted in one of these XML files, which makes them the authoritative record of which OEM apps hold elevated permissions. A large or vendor-heavy allowlist is where over-privileged OEM software becomes visible. Informational because every device has one and the size is build-specific.
checks.remediation: Read the allowlist files and check each granted permission against what the app genuinely needs, paying particular attention to vendor and product partition entries which receive less scrutiny than the AOSP set.

checks.label: Dalvik Cache Not World-Writable
checks.command: W=$(ls -ld /data/dalvik-cache /data/dalvik-cache/*/ 2>/dev/null | grep -cE "^d.{7}w"); N=$(find /data/dalvik-cache -maxdepth 2 -perm -o+w 2>/dev/null | wc -l); D=$(find /data/dalvik-cache -maxdepth 2 2>&1 1>/dev/null | grep -c "Permission denied"); if [ "$W" -gt 0 ] || [ "$N" -gt 0 ]; then echo "WORLD_WRITABLE dirs=$W files=$N"; elif [ "$D" -gt 0 ]; then echo "UNMEASURED dirs_checked_clean enumeration_denied=$D"; else echo CLEAN; fi
checks.description: Finds world-writable entries in the dalvik-cache, which holds the ahead-of-time compiled ART artifacts (odex, vdex, art) that the runtime maps and executes. A writable cache entry means an unprivileged process can replace compiled code that a privileged process will execute on next start, which is arbitrary code execution across a privilege boundary without needing a memory corruption bug. On a healthy device this returns nothing.
checks.remediation: Remove world write permission from every entry listed and investigate how it was set. Wipe and regenerate the cache with 'cmd package compile -r bg-dexopt -a' after correcting the permissions.
checks.why: Replacing a compiled ART artifact substitutes code that a privileged process executes at startup.
checks.risk_if_fail: Arbitrary code execution in the context of any process whose compiled artifacts were replaced.

checks.label: APK Signature Scheme Distribution
checks.command: V=$(dumpsys package 2>/dev/null | grep -oE 'apkSigningVersion=[0-9]+' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{printf "v%s=%s ", substr($2,18), $1}'); I=$(find /data/app -maxdepth 4 -name '*.idsig' 2>/dev/null | wc -l); [ -z "$V" ] && echo "NO_SIGNING_INFO idsig_files=${I:-0}" || echo "$V idsig_files=${I:-0}"
checks.description: Reports how many installed packages use each APK signature scheme and how many carry a v4 .idsig file. Scheme v2 and v3 sign the archive itself rather than individual entries, closing the Janus and Master Key class of forgery that v1 permitted. Scheme v4 pairs with fs-verity to allow incremental installation while still verifying every block on read. This complements the existing v1-only check by showing the whole distribution rather than only the worst case, so an auditor can see how much of the install base predates modern signing.
checks.remediation: Ensure in-house apps are signed with v2 or later, and prefer v3 so signing-key rotation is possible without breaking updates. Investigate any package still relying on v1 alone.

checks.label: Package Rollback and Downgrade Protection
checks.command: R=$(dumpsys rollback 2>/dev/null | head -20); if [ -z "$R" ]; then echo NO_ROLLBACK_SERVICE; else A=$(printf '%s' "$R" | grep -ci 'rollbackId'); echo "rollback_service=present available_rollbacks=${A:-0}"; fi
checks.description: Reports the state of the RollbackManager, which stages the previous version of an app or APEX so a bad update can be reverted. The security question is the inverse of the reliability one: a staged rollback is a copy of an older, potentially vulnerable build kept on the device, and a downgrade path that does not verify the target version lets an attacker reintroduce a patched vulnerability. Informational because rollback availability is a deliberate platform feature and its presence is not a misconfiguration.
checks.remediation: Confirm rollbacks expire as expected and that no rollback retains a build with a known unpatched vulnerability. On a managed fleet, prefer disabling user-initiated rollback.

checks.label: Split APK and Staged Install Sessions
checks.command: S=$(find /data/app -maxdepth 4 -name 'split_*.apk' 2>/dev/null | wc -l); T=$(pm list staged-sessions 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'sessionId'); [ -z "$T" ] && T=0; echo "split_apks=${S:-0} staged_sessions=$T"
checks.description: Counts split APK files and staged install sessions. A split APK is verified as part of its base package, but a session left staged is a pending install that will be applied at next reboot, and on a device being audited it means code is queued to run that is not yet reflected in the installed package list. A staged session is normal briefly during an OTA or a Play update, so a non-zero count on an idle device is worth explaining rather than assuming benign.
checks.remediation: Inspect any staged session with 'pm list staged-sessions' and abandon unexpected ones with 'pm install-abandon <id>'. Re-audit after the pending install has been applied.
checks.why: A staged session is code queued to install at next boot that no package listing yet reflects.
checks.risk_if_fail: The device will apply an install after reboot that the audit did not evaluate.

checks.label: Exported Components Without Permission (Third-Party)
checks.command: D=$(dumpsys package 2>/dev/null); if [ -z "$D" ]; then echo NO_PACKAGE_DUMP; else E=$(printf '%s' "$D" | grep -c 'exported=true'); P=$(printf '%s' "$D" | grep -c 'permission='); echo "exported_components=${E:-0} with_permission_decl=${P:-0}"; fi
checks.description: Counts components declared exported and how many permission declarations appear alongside them. An exported activity, service, receiver or provider is an IPC entry point any other app can reach, and one without a permission guard is reachable by any installed app with no user consent. This is the entry point for the intent redirection, deep link hijacking and confused deputy classes. Reported as a count for review rather than a pass or fail because every app legitimately exports its launcher activity and the ratio is meaningless without knowing which packages are involved. Use 'dumpsys package <pkg>' to drill into any package of concern.
checks.remediation: For every third-party or in-house package, review its exported components and add a signature-level permission or set exported=false where cross-app access is not required. Pay particular attention to exported providers with grantUriPermissions.

checks.label: Secret Code Dialer Receivers (OEM Service Menus)
checks.command: D=$(dumpsys package 2>/dev/null | grep -B8 -i 'SECRET_CODE' | grep -oE '^[ ]*[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+/[a-zA-Z0-9_.$]+' | sort -u | head -15); [ -z "$D" ] && echo NO_SECRET_CODE_RECEIVERS || printf '%s\n' "$D"
checks.description: Lists components registered for the android.provider.Telephony.SECRET_CODE broadcast, which is how dialer codes of the form *#*#nnnn#*#* reach an application. OEMs use these to open service menus, field test modes, radio diagnostics, factory test suites and hidden logging controls. Anyone who can reach the dialer, including someone with brief physical access to a locked-down kiosk or POS terminal that still exposes a dialer, can trigger them, and the receiving component often runs with system privilege. Reported for review because the legitimate set is entirely OEM-specific.
checks.remediation: Enumerate each receiver and determine what its code exposes. Remove or disable factory test, field test and diagnostic receivers on production and kiosk builds, and confirm none can be reached without authentication.
